cse-2013-cs-45.approach: Pipeline clock = slowest stage + buffer delay. Only 8 instructions (I1–I4, I9–I12) complete; with no branch prediction, the fetch of I9 waits until I4 finishes its EI stage, which costs 3 bubble cycles.
cse-2013-cs-45.given:
| Stage | FI | DI | FO | EI | WO |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Delay (ns) | 5 | 7 | 10 | 8 | 6 |

Buffer delay 1 ns; 12 instructions; I4 branches to I9 (taken).

steps.title: Cycle time
steps.body:
Every stage must fit the slowest stage plus its latch:
$$t_c = \max(5,7,10,8,6) + 1 = 10 + 1 = 11\text{ ns}$$

scene.caption: I1–I4 enter one per cycle; I4 is the branch

steps.title: When the branch resolves
steps.body: I4 starts in cycle 4, so its stages are FI(4), DI(5), FO(6), EI(7). The target address is known only at the end of EI, i.e. cycle 7. Without prediction nothing useful can be fetched in cycles 5, 6, 7, so I9 is fetched in cycle 8 — a penalty of **3 cycles**.

steps.title: Count the cycles
steps.body:
Executed instructions: I1, I2, I3, I4, I9, I10, I11, I12 = 8.
$$\text{cycles} = (k + n - 1) + \text{stalls} = (5 + 8 - 1) + 3 = 15$$
I12 is fetched in cycle 11 and writes back in cycle $11+4 = 15$.

steps.title: Total time
steps.body: $$T = 15 \times 11 = 165\text{ ns}$$

optionAnalysis.reason: 132 = 12 × 11: counts 12 cycles, i.e. 8 instructions with no branch penalty (and even then 12 ≠ 5 + 8 − 1).

176 = 16 × 11: one cycle too many (e.g. counting a 4-cycle penalty).
328 ns is roughly a non-pipelined estimate (8 instructions × 41 ns) — ignores pipelining.

cse-2013-cs-45.shortcut: Branch resolved in stage $s$ ⇒ penalty $s-1$ cycles. Here $s=4$ (EI), so $T = (5+8-1+3)\times 11$.

Forgetting the 1 ns buffer delay.

steps.body:

- 4 decoders on the leaves give $4\times4 = 16$ outputs (driven by 2 address bits),
- 1 decoder drives their 4 enable lines (other 2 address bits).

Total $= 4 + 1 = 5$.

7 would be needed only for a deeper tree than 16 outputs require.

pitfalls: Decoding 32 chips individually — chips in the same row are selected together.
Forgetting the top-level decoder that drives the enables.

cse-2013-cs-48.approach: Use code motion to delay d and e into the else-branch (the only place they are used), then check the largest set of simultaneously live values. If it still exceeds two, at least one spill is unavoidable.

steps.title: Move d and e where they are used
Live values after x = c * c
steps.body: After computing x, we still need $x$ (for the test), $a$ (test and both branches) and $c$ (for d and e in the else-branch): $\{a, c, x\}$ = 3 values. With only 2 registers one of them must go to memory, so **at least 1 spill**.

steps.title: One spill is enough
steps.body:
Schedule with registers R1, R2 (loading a or b from memory is not a spill):
1. R1 = a, R2 = b; R2 = R1 + R2 (c)
2. **store c** (the only spill); R2 = R2 * R2 (x); compare R2 > R1
3. then: R1 = R1 * R1 (y)
4. else: R2 = load c; R2 = R2 * R1 (d); R2 = R2 * R2 (d·d, dead afterwards); R2 = load c; R1 = R2 + R1 (e); R1 = R1 * R1

Reloading c needs no further store, so the minimum is **1**.

Exactly one spill (of c) suffices after code motion.
2 spills are needed only without moving d and e into the else-branch.
3 overcounts; code motion removes most of the pressure.

pitfalls: Treating the code as fixed — code motion is allowed and is the whole point.
Forgetting that x must be live until the if-test.
cse-2013-cs-48.verification: Max live set after motion: {a, c, x} = 3 at one point only, so 3 − 2 = 1 value has to be stored once.

cse-2013-cs-50.approach: The flaw: after A[i] is replaced by newc[j], the inner loop keeps going, so the new character can match a later oldc[k] (k > j) and be replaced again. A test case exposes it only if some newc[j] equals some oldc[k] with k > j.

steps.title: Condition for the flaw
steps.body: A character $A[i]=oldc[j]$ becomes $newc[j]$; it is wrongly re-replaced iff $newc[j] = oldc[k]$ for some $k > j$. With all strings over {a,…,e} tried, a test case catches the flaw iff this condition holds for some $j$.

steps.title: Check each test case
steps.body:
| Test | oldc | newc | chained? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | abc | dab | a→d (d not later in oldc), b→a (a is earlier), c→b (none later): **no** |
| 2 | cde | bcd | c→b, d→c (c earlier), e→d (earlier): **no** |
| 3 | bca | cda | b→c and c = oldc[1]: **yes** (b→c→d) |
| 4 | abc | bac | a→b and b = oldc[1]: **yes** (a→b→a) |

cse-2013-cs-52.approach: Each table level fits in one page, so every level resolves (page size / PTE size) entries. Equate the virtual address width to offset bits + 3 × index bits.

steps.title: Set up
steps.body: Let page size $= 2^p$ bytes. PTE $= 32$ bits $= 4$ B, so a page holds $2^{p}/2^{2} = 2^{p-2}$ entries ⇒ each level indexes $p-2$ bits.

steps.title: Solve
steps.body:
$$46 = p + 3(p-2) \Rightarrow 46 = 4p - 6 \Rightarrow p = 13$$
Page size $= 2^{13}$ B $= 8$ KB.

pitfalls: Using PTE = 32 bytes instead of 32 bits.
cse-2013-cs-52.verification: Plug back: offset 13 bits, three 11-bit indices (2048 entries × 4 B = 8 KB per table page). $13+33=46$ ✓.

steps.title: Bits beyond the page offset
steps.body:
Page offset $= 13$ bits (8 KB page from Q52). Index bits taken from the virtual page number $= 16 - 13 = 3$.
$$\text{colours} = 2^{3} = 8$$

16 would follow from a 4 KB page (16 − 12 = 4 bits).

Forgetting the associativity when computing sets.

- $B^+ = B\,CFH\,EG\,A = ABCEFGH$
